Physiology-02.question: ১) Food intake is regulated by
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is circulating level of leptin. Food intake is regulated mainly by the hypothalamus, where leptin acts as a signal of body energy stores.

  • High leptin levels (after increased fat storage) → inhibit appetite by activating satiety pathways.

  • Low leptin levels → stimulate hunger and food intake.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thermostatic mechanism – Regulates body temperature, not food intake.

  • Specific dynamic action of food – Refers to increased energy expenditure after eating (thermic effect of food).

  • Basal metabolic rate – Determines resting energy expenditure, not direct control of appetite.

High-yield points:

Regulation of food intake:

  • Hypothalamus

    • Lateral hypothalamus → hunger centre

    • Ventromedial hypothalamus → satiety centre

  • Leptin → decreases appetite

  • Ghrelin → increases appetite

Exam pearl:
Leptin level reflects fat stores and regulates appetite.

Physiology-02.question: ২) Water is absorbed in the jejunum, ileum, and colon and excreted in the feces. Arrange these in order of the amount of water absorbed or excreted from the greatest to the smallest.
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is jejunum → ileum → colon → feces.

Most water absorption occurs in the small intestine, especially the jejunum, because it receives the largest volume of fluid from gastric and intestinal secretions.

Approximate daily water handling:

  • Jejunum → absorbs the greatest amount of water

  • Ileum → absorbs the remaining significant amount

  • Colon → absorbs residual water and concentrates feces

  • Feces → contains only a small amount of water excreted

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Colon first – Although the colon absorbs water efficiently, the total amount absorbed is much less than the jejunum.

  • Feces first – Feces contain the least amount of water.

High-yield points:

Water absorption order:

Jejunum > Ileum > Colon > Feces

Exam pearl:
Small intestine absorbs most water; colon mainly concentrates stool.

Physiology-02.question: ৩) Which of the following has the highest pH?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is pancreatic juice. Pancreatic secretion has the highest pH (≈7.8–8.5) due to a high concentration of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) secreted by pancreatic duct cells. It neutralizes acidic gastric chyme entering the duodenum.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gastric juice – Highly acidic due to HCl (pH ≈ 1–3).

  • Colonic luminal contents – Slightly acidic to neutral due to bacterial fermentation (pH ≈ 5.5–7).

  • Contents of intestinal crypts – Usually alkaline but less alkaline than pancreatic juice.

High-yield points:

Fluid Approximate pH
Gastric juice 1–3
Pancreatic juice 7.8–8.5 (highest)
Bile 7–8
Intestinal juice 7–8

Exam pearl:
Most alkaline digestive secretion = pancreatic juice (bicarbonate-rich).

Physiology-02.question: ৪) In infants, defecation often follows a meal. The cause of colonic contractions in this situation is -?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is the gastrocolic reflex. In infants, feeding stimulates gastric distension, which triggers increased colonic motility and mass movements, leading to defecation soon after a meal.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Increased circulating levels of CCK – CCK mainly causes gallbladder contraction, pancreatic enzyme secretion, and slowing of gastric emptying; it is not the main cause of post-meal defecation.

  • Increased circulating levels of somatostatin – Somatostatin inhibits gastrointestinal secretion and motility.

  • Enterogastric reflex – Inhibits gastric activity when chyme enters the small intestine; it does not stimulate colonic contractions.

High-yield points:

Gastrocolic reflex:

  • Gastric distension after food intake → increased colonic motility

  • Stronger in infants

  • Responsible for defecation after meals

Exam pearl:
Meal → stomach stretch → colon contraction → defecation = Gastrocolic reflex.

Physiology-02.question: ৫) The migrating motor complex is triggered by which of the following?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is motilin. The migrating motor complex (MMC) is a cyclic pattern of gastrointestinal smooth muscle contractions that occurs during the fasting state and is initiated mainly by motilin released from the small intestine.

Functions of MMC:

  • Sweeps residual food particles and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine

  • Acts as a “housekeeping wave” of the GI tract

  • Occurs approximately every 90–120 minutes during fasting

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CCK – Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction; slows gastric emptying after meals.

  • Somatostatin – Inhibits many GI hormones and decreases motility.

  • Secretin – Stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and inhibits gastric acid secretion.

High-yield points:

Hormone Main function
Motilin Migrating motor complex (MMC)
CCK Gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzymes
Secretin Pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion
Somatostatin Inhibitory GI hormone

Exam pearl:
Fasting motility pattern = MMC = Motilin

Physiology-02.question: ৬) Which of the following hormones acts on its target tissues by a steroid hormone mechanism of action?
Physiology-02.option3: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on the collecting duct
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) act by a steroid hormone-like mechanism:

  • They are lipid-soluble.

  • Enter target cells by diffusion/transport.

  • Bind to intracellular nuclear receptors.

  • Alter gene transcription and protein synthesis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Parathyroid hormone (PTH) – Acts through a cell membrane receptor (GPCR) → activates cAMP second messenger pathway.

  • Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on collecting duct – Acts mainly via V2 receptors (GPCR) → cAMP pathway → insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.

  • Glucagon – Acts through a GPCR → cAMP second messenger system.

High-yield points:

Hormone type Mechanism
Steroid hormones Intracellular/nuclear receptor → gene transcription
Thyroid hormone (T3/T4) Nuclear receptor (steroid-like)
Peptide hormones (PTH, ADH, glucagon) Membrane receptors → second messengers

Exam pearl:
Thyroid hormone behaves like steroid hormones despite being an amine-derived hormone.

Physiology-02.question: ৭) Which of the following hormones originates in the anterior pituitary?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). TSH is a tropic hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) and stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T3 and T4.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dopamine – Produced mainly by the hypothalamus; inhibits prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary.

  • Growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH) – Secreted by the hypothalamus; stimulates GH release.

  • Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) – Secreted by the hypothalamus; stimulates LH and FSH release.

High-yield points:

Anterior pituitary hormones (FLAT PiG):

  • F → FSH

  • L → LH

  • A → ACTH

  • T → TSH

  • P → Prolactin

  • iG → Growth hormone (IGF-1 related)

Exam pearl:
TSH is a pituitary hormone; GHRH and GnRH are hypothalamic hormones.

Physiology-02.question: ৮) Which of the following inhibits the secretion of growth hormone by the anterior pituitary?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is somatomedins (IGF-1). Growth hormone (GH) secretion from the anterior pituitary is inhibited by negative feedback from somatomedins, especially insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) produced mainly by the liver.

The other options are incorrect because they increase GH secretion:

  • Sleep – Deep (slow-wave) sleep stimulates GH release.

  • Stress – Physical and emotional stress increase GH secretion.

  • Puberty – Increased sex steroids during puberty stimulate GH secretion, contributing to growth spurt.

High-yield points:

Factors increasing GH:

  • Deep sleep

  • Exercise

  • Stress

  • Fasting/hypoglycaemia

  • Puberty

Factors decreasing GH:

  • Somatomedin (IGF-1) feedback

  • Hyperglycaemia

  • Increased free fatty acids

Exam pearl:
IGF-1 (somatomedin) provides negative feedback to inhibit GH secretion.

Physiology-02.question: ৯) Selective destruction of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex would produce a deficiency of which hormone?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is aldosterone. The zona glomerulosa is the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex and is responsible for producing mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone.

The other options are incorrect because they are produced by other adrenal cortical zones:

  • Androstenedione – Produced mainly by the zona reticularis (and gonads).

  • Cortisol – Produced by the zona fasciculata.

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) – Produced by the zona reticularis.

High-yield points:

Adrenal cortex layers (outer → inner):

GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex

Zone Hormone
Zona Glomerulosa Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone)
Zona Fasciculata Cortisol (Glucocorticoids)
Zona Reticularis Androgens (DHEA, androstenedione)

Exam pearl:
Glomerulosa = Aldosterone = Salt regulation.

Physiology-02.question: ১০) Which of the following decreases the conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is chronic renal failure. Conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol) to the active form 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol) occurs in the kidney by the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase.

In chronic renal failure, damaged renal tissue causes:

  • ↓ 1α-hydroxylase activity

  • ↓ calcitriol production

  • ↓ intestinal calcium absorption

  • Secondary hyperparathyroidism

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypocalcemia – Stimulates PTH release, which increases renal 1α-hydroxylase activity and calcitriol formation.

  • Hyperparathyroidism – PTH stimulates conversion to calcitriol.

  • Hypophosphatemia – Stimulates calcitriol production.

High-yield points:

Factors increasing calcitriol formation:

  • ↑ PTH

  • ↓ Calcium

  • ↓ Phosphate

Factors decreasing calcitriol formation:

  • Chronic renal failure

  • Reduced renal 1α-hydroxylase activity

Exam pearl:
Kidney failure → ↓ calcitriol → renal osteodystrophy.

Physiology-02.question: ১১) Which of the following causes increased aldosterone secretion?
Physiology-02.option2: Administration of an inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is decreased blood volume. A fall in blood volume decreases renal perfusion pressure, activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS):

↓ Blood volume → ↓ Renal perfusion → ↑ Renin → ↑ Angiotensin II → ↑ Aldosterone secretion

Aldosterone increases:

  • Na⁺ reabsorption

  • Water retention

  • K⁺ secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Administration of an ACE inhibitor – Blocks formation of angiotensin II → decreases aldosterone secretion.

  • Hyperosmolarity – Mainly stimulates ADH secretion and thirst, not aldosterone.

  • Hypokalemia – Suppresses aldosterone secretion; hyperkalemia stimulates aldosterone release.

High-yield points:

Stimulators of aldosterone:

  • ↓ Blood volume / ↓ BP

  • ↑ Renin

  • ↑ Angiotensin II

  • ↑ Plasma K⁺

Inhibitors of aldosterone:

  • ACE inhibitors

  • Angiotensin receptor blockers

  • Hypokalemia

Exam pearl:
Low blood volume → RAAS activation → increased aldosterone.

Physiology-02.question: ১২) Secretion of oxytocin is increased by-?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is dilation of the cervix. Oxytocin secretion from the posterior pituitary is increased by cervical stretching during labour through the Ferguson reflex:

Cervical dilation → sensory impulses to hypothalamus → ↑ oxytocin release → uterine contraction → further cervical dilation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Milk ejection – Oxytocin causes milk ejection, but the stimulus for oxytocin release is nipple stimulation/suckling, not milk ejection itself.

  • Increased prolactin levels – Prolactin promotes milk production but does not directly stimulate oxytocin secretion.

  • Increased extracellular fluid (ECF) volume – Stimulates release of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), not oxytocin.

High-yield points:

Oxytocin secretion increases with:

  • Cervical dilation (Ferguson reflex)

  • Nipple stimulation during breastfeeding

Oxytocin functions:

  • Uterine contraction during labour

  • Milk ejection (let-down reflex)

Exam pearl:
Cervical stretch → oxytocin release → stronger uterine contraction.

Physiology-02.question: ১৩) Which of the following pancreatic secretions has a receptor with four subunits, two of which have tyrosine kinase activity?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is insulin. The insulin receptor is a tetrameric receptor (α₂β₂ structure):

  • Two α subunits → extracellular, bind insulin

  • Two β subunits → intracellular, contain tyrosine kinase activity

Binding of insulin activates the receptor tyrosine kinase pathway, leading to phosphorylation cascades and metabolic effects.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glucagon – Acts through a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) → activates adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP.

  • Somatostatin – Acts through GPCRs → inhibits hormone secretion.

  • Pancreatic lipase – An enzyme, not a hormone; does not have a receptor.

High-yield points:

Hormone Receptor type
Insulin Receptor tyrosine kinase (α₂β₂)
Glucagon GPCR → cAMP
Somatostatin GPCR → inhibitory pathway
GH JAK-STAT pathway

Exam pearl:
Insulin receptor = 4 subunits + tyrosine kinase activity.

Physiology-02.question: ১৪) Which of the following substances is released from neurons in the GI tract and produces smooth muscle relaxation?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). VIP is a neurotransmitter released from enteric neurons that causes:

  • Relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle

  • Relaxation of gastrointestinal sphincters

  • Increased intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes

  • Vasodilation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Secretin – A hormone from duodenal S cells that stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and inhibits gastric acid secretion.

  • Gastrin – A hormone from G cells that stimulates gastric acid secretion and increases gastric motility.

  • Cholecystokinin (CCK) – Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, gallbladder contraction, and slows gastric emptying.

High-yield points:

Substance Main action
VIP GI smooth muscle relaxation
Gastrin ↑ HCl secretion
Secretin ↑ Pancreatic HCO₃⁻
CCK ↑ Pancreatic enzymes + gallbladder contraction

Exam pearl:
VIP = “Very Important for relaxation” of GI smooth muscle.

Physiology-02.question: ১৫) Which of the following is the site of Na+–bile acid cotransport?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is ileum. The terminal ileum is the site of Na⁺–bile acid cotransport through the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT).

This mechanism is responsible for enterohepatic circulation:

Bile acids → absorbed in terminal ileum → transported back to liver via portal circulation → reused in bile formation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gastric antrum – Mainly involved in gastrin secretion and gastric acid regulation.

  • Gastric fundus – Contains parietal cells for HCl and intrinsic factor secretion.

  • Duodenum – Site of mixing of bile with chyme and pancreatic secretion, but not the main site of bile acid absorption.

High-yield points:

Bile acid absorption:

  • Site → Terminal ileum

  • Transport → Na⁺-bile acid cotransporter (ASBT)

  • Failure → bile acid loss → diarrhea + fat malabsorption

Exam pearl:
Terminal ileum = bile acid and vitamin B12 absorption site.

Physiology-02.question: ১৬) Which promotes uterine contraction?
১৭) Which hormone increases renal sodium reabsorption?
১৮) Which stimulates secretion of uterine milk?
১৯) Excess GH secretion during adulthood may result in
২০) Amino acid required for thyroid hormone synthesis
২১) Sites of action of PTH excludes
২২) The entire period of spermatogenesis takes about -
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 74 days. The process of spermatogenesis (development of spermatogonia into mature spermatozoa) takes approximately 74 days in humans.

After formation, sperm require additional time for:

  • Epididymal maturation and storage → about 10–14 days

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 73 days – Close but not the standard accepted value.

  • 75 days – Sometimes quoted due to variation, but 74 days is the classic physiology value.

  • 76 days – Not the standard duration.

High-yield points:

Spermatogenesis:

  • Site → Seminiferous tubules of testes

  • Duration → ~74 days

  • Requires → FSH, testosterone, Sertoli cells

Exam pearl:
Spermatogenesis = 74 days; sperm maturation in epididymis = additional ~10–14 days.

Physiology-02.question: ২৩) Which gut hormone causes relaxation of sphincter of Oddi?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is CCK. Cholecystokinin, released from I cells of the duodenum and jejunum, causes:

  • Contraction of the gallbladder

  • Relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi

  • Release of bile into the duodenum

  • Increased pancreatic enzyme secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gastrin – Stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric motility.

  • Secretin – Stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and inhibits gastric acid secretion; does not primarily relax the sphincter of Oddi.

  • Ghrelin – Stimulates appetite and promotes growth hormone release.

High-yield points:

CCK actions:

  • ↑ Gallbladder contraction

  • ↓ Sphincter of Oddi tone

  • ↑ Pancreatic enzyme secretion

  • ↓ Gastric emptying

Exam pearl:
CCK = Gallbladder squeeze + Oddi relaxation.

Physiology-02.question: ২৪) Satiety producing hormone is-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is leptin. Leptin is a satiety hormone produced mainly by adipose tissue. It acts on the hypothalamus to reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ghrelin – A hunger hormone secreted mainly from the stomach; increases appetite.

  • Adiponectin – An adipokine involved in insulin sensitivity and metabolism, not a major satiety hormone.

  • Cortisol – A stress hormone that can increase appetite and does not act as a satiety signal.

High-yield points:

Hormone Effect on appetite
Leptin ↓ Appetite (satiety)
Ghrelin ↑ Appetite (hunger)
Insulin ↓ Appetite (central effect)
CCK Promotes short-term satiety

Exam pearl:
Leptin = long-term satiety signal from fat stores.

Physiology-02.question: ২৫) Major humoral mediator of gall bladder contraction in response to fat meal is-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is CCK. Cholecystokinin is the major humoral mediator of gallbladder contraction after a fat-containing meal.

Fat and amino acids in the duodenum → stimulation of I cells → release of CCK →

  • Gallbladder contraction

  • Relaxation of sphincter of Oddi

  • Bile release into duodenum

  • Pancreatic enzyme secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Secretin – Mainly stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and bile duct bicarbonate secretion.

  • Gastrin – Stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric motility.

  • Somatostatin – Inhibits gastrointestinal hormone secretion and motility.

High-yield points:

CCK actions:

  • ↑ Gallbladder contraction

  • ↓ Sphincter of Oddi tone

  • ↑ Pancreatic enzyme secretion

  • ↓ Gastric emptying

Exam pearl:
Fat in duodenum → CCK release → gallbladder contraction.

Physiology-02.question: ২৬) Main site of absorption of vit B12 is-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is terminal ileum. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) absorption occurs mainly in the terminal ileum after it binds with intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells.

Process:

  • Vitamin B12 + intrinsic factor → complex formation

  • Absorbed by specific receptors in terminal ileum

  • Transported to blood bound to transcobalamin

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Upper jejunum – Absorbs many nutrients but not vitamin B12.

  • Upper duodenum – Site of iron and calcium absorption.

  • Large intestine – Mainly absorbs water and electrolytes; not B12.

High-yield points:

Vitamin B12 absorption:

  • Source of intrinsic factor → Parietal cells of stomach

  • Absorption site → Terminal ileum

  • Defect → Pernicious anaemia, ileal disease/resection

Exam pearl:
Terminal ileum absorbs both Vitamin B12 and bile acids.

Physiology-02.question: ২৭) HCL is secreted from-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is oxyntic cell. Oxyntic (parietal) cells of the gastric glands secrete:

  • Hydrochloric acid (HCl)

  • Intrinsic factor (required for vitamin B12 absorption)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Chief cell – Secretes pepsinogen and gastric lipase.

  • G-cell – Secretes gastrin, which stimulates HCl secretion indirectly by acting on parietal cells.

  • Mucus neck cell – Secretes mucus for gastric mucosal protection.

High-yield points:

Gastric cell Secretion
Oxyntic (parietal) cell HCl + Intrinsic factor
Chief cell Pepsinogen
G-cell Gastrin
Mucous neck cell Mucus

Exam pearl:

Physiology-02.question: ২৮) Intrinsic factor of castle is present in-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is gastric juice. Intrinsic factor of Castle is secreted by the parietal (oxyntic) cells of the gastric mucosa and is therefore present in gastric juice.

Intrinsic factor is essential for:

  • Binding vitamin B12

  • Absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Saliva – Contains enzymes and mucus but not intrinsic factor.

  • Succus entericus – Intestinal juice; contains digestive enzymes but not intrinsic factor.

  • Pancreatic juice – Contains digestive enzymes and bicarbonate, not intrinsic factor.

High-yield points:

Intrinsic factor:

  • Secreted by → Parietal cells (oxyntic cells) of stomach

  • Present in → Gastric juice

  • Function → Vitamin B12 absorption in terminal ileum

Exam pearl:
Loss of intrinsic factor → pernicious anaemia.

Physiology-02.question: ২৯) Tetany occurs when plasma calcium level falls below …mg/dl
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 5 mg/dL. Tetany occurs when plasma ionized calcium levels fall significantly, and clinically it is usually seen when total serum calcium falls below approximately 7–8 mg/dL, with classic physiology MCQs often using 5 mg/dL as the critical level.

Low calcium increases neuronal excitability by reducing the threshold for action potential generation, causing:

  • Perioral tingling

  • Muscle cramps

  • Carpopedal spasm

  • Chvostek and Trousseau signs

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 4 mg/dL – Too low; represents severe hypocalcaemia.

  • 6 mg/dL – Low calcium but not the classic threshold used in this MCQ.

  • 9 mg/dL – Within the normal serum calcium range (≈8.5–10.5 mg/dL).

High-yield points:

Normal serum calcium: ~8.5–10.5 mg/dL
Tetany: classically when serum calcium falls markedly, around <5–7 mg/dL (depending on whether total or ionized calcium is considered).

Exam pearl:
Severe hypocalcaemia → tetany.

Physiology-02.question: ৩০) Catecholamines are derived from
৩১) The most active adrenal androgen is
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is testosterone. Among adrenal androgens, testosterone is the most biologically active androgen, although the adrenal cortex mainly secretes weaker androgens such as DHEA and androstenedione, which can be converted peripherally into testosterone.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) – A weak adrenal androgen and a precursor of more active androgens.

  • Androstenedione – A weak androgen precursor that can be converted to testosterone.

  • Cortisol – A glucocorticoid produced by zona fasciculata; not an androgen.

High-yield points:

Adrenal cortex androgen production:

  • Zona reticularis → DHEA, androstenedione

  • Peripheral conversion → testosterone

Relative androgen activity:
Testosterone > Androstenedione > DHEA

Exam pearl:
Most active androgen = Testosterone; main adrenal androgen = DHEA.

Physiology-02.question: ৩২) D cell of islets of Langerhans secrete
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is somatostatin. D cells (δ-cells) of the islets of Langerhans secrete somatostatin, which inhibits the secretion of several pancreatic and gastrointestinal hormones.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Insulin – Secreted by β-cells of pancreatic islets.

  • Glucagon – Secreted by α-cells of pancreatic islets.

  • PP (pancreatic polypeptide) – Secreted by PP/F cells of pancreatic islets.

High-yield points:

Islet cell Hormone
β-cell Insulin
α-cell Glucagon
δ-cell (D-cell) Somatostatin
PP/F-cell Pancreatic polypeptide

Exam pearl:
D-cell = Somatostatin = “D” for Delta.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৩) Diabetogenic hormone
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is growth hormone (GH). GH is called a diabetogenic hormone because it has anti-insulin effects:

  • ↓ Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle and adipose tissue

  • ↑ Lipolysis

  • ↑ Blood glucose level

  • Promotes insulin resistance

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ADH – Regulates water balance and urine concentration; not diabetogenic.

  • Insulin – An anti-diabetogenic hormone because it lowers blood glucose.

  • Oxytocin – Causes uterine contraction and milk ejection; no major effect on glucose regulation.

High-yield points:

Diabetogenic hormones (counter-regulatory hormones):

  • GH

  • Cortisol

  • Glucagon

  • Catecholamines

Exam pearl:
GH excess → insulin resistance → hyperglycaemia (diabetogenic effect).

Physiology-02.question: ৩৪) Ovulation occurs at day
৩৫) Which hormone has receptor on membrane?
৩৬) Which hormone has anti-inflammatory effect?
৩৭) Major anabolic hormone of the body is-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is insulin. Insulin is considered the major anabolic hormone of the body because it promotes storage and synthesis of nutrients:

  • ↑ Glucose uptake into cells

  • ↑ Glycogen synthesis

  • ↑ Fat synthesis (lipogenesis)

  • ↑ Protein synthesis

  • ↓ Protein breakdown

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Growth hormone – Has anabolic effects, especially on growth via IGF-1, but is not the major anabolic hormone of metabolism.

  • Thyroid hormone – Mainly increases metabolic rate and energy expenditure.

  • Aldosterone – Regulates sodium and potassium balance, not anabolic metabolism.

High-yield points:

Insulin = anabolic hormone

  • Carbohydrate → glycogen storage

  • Fat → triglyceride storage

  • Protein → amino acid uptake and synthesis

Exam pearl:
Major anabolic hormone = Insulin; major catabolic hormones = cortisol, glucagon, catecholamines.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৮) The Permissive action of cortisol is on-
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is glucagon. Cortisol has a permissive action on glucagon by allowing glucagon to exert its full effects on glucose metabolism.

Cortisol:

  • Increases hepatic enzyme synthesis needed for gluconeogenesis

  • Enhances the hyperglycaemic effect of glucagon

  • Helps maintain blood glucose during stress

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thyroxine – Has metabolic effects but is not the classic example of cortisol permissive action.

  • Aldosterone – Cortisol does not have a permissive action on aldosterone secretion.

  • Growth hormone – Cortisol may interact metabolically, but the classic permissive effect is with catecholamines and glucagon.

High-yield points:

Permissive effects of cortisol:

  • Catecholamines → maintains vascular response to adrenaline/noradrenaline

  • Glucagon → promotes gluconeogenesis and hyperglycaemia

Exam pearl:
Cortisol permits glucagon action and maintains catecholamine responsiveness.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৯) Which of the following hormone is called “Stress Hormone”?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is cortisol. Cortisol is called the “stress hormone” because its secretion increases during physical and psychological stress and helps the body adapt.

Major actions of cortisol during stress:

  • ↑ Blood glucose by gluconeogenesis

  • ↑ Protein breakdown

  • ↑ Lipolysis

  • Maintains blood pressure by increasing vascular responsiveness to catecholamines

  • Suppresses excessive inflammation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • PTH – Regulates calcium and phosphate balance.

  • Aldosterone – Regulates sodium and potassium balance and fluid volume.

  • Thyroxine – Regulates basal metabolic rate and growth.

High-yield points:

Stress response hormones:

  • Cortisol → major stress hormone

  • Catecholamines → acute stress response (“fight or flight”)

Exam pearl:
Cortisol = stress hormone + anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid.

Physiology-02.question: ৪০) Which of the following hormone is called “Life Saving Hormone”?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is cortisol. Cortisol is called a “life-saving hormone” because it is essential for survival, especially during stressful conditions such as trauma, infection, and shock.

Functions that make cortisol life-sustaining:

  • Maintains vascular tone and blood pressure

  • Enhances response to catecholamines

  • Maintains blood glucose through gluconeogenesis

  • Modulates immune and inflammatory responses

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ADH – Maintains water balance and prevents excessive water loss, but is not classically termed the life-saving hormone.

  • Aldosterone – Maintains sodium and potassium balance; deficiency causes salt wasting and hypotension.

  • Insulin – Essential for glucose regulation, but not called the “life-saving hormone” in physiology.

High-yield points:

Cortisol:

  • Stress hormone

  • Life-saving hormone

  • Anti-inflammatory hormone

  • Glucocorticoid from zona fasciculata

Exam pearl:
Cortisol is essential for survival during severe stress and shock.

Physiology-02.question: ৪১) Which hormone prevents involution of corpus follicles?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is hCG. During early pregnancy, hCG prevents involution of the corpus luteum (corpus luteum of pregnancy) by maintaining its function.

hCG:

  • Acts like LH

  • Maintains corpus luteum

  • Stimulates continued secretion of progesterone

  • Maintains the endometrium for pregnancy until the placenta takes over hormone production

The other options are incorrect because:

  • FSH – Stimulates follicular development but does not maintain the corpus luteum.

  • LH – Maintains corpus luteum in the normal menstrual cycle, but during pregnancy this role is replaced by hCG.

  • Inhibin – Inhibits FSH secretion; does not maintain corpus luteum.

High-yield points:

Pregnancy hormones:

  • hCG → maintains corpus luteum

  • Progesterone → maintains endometrium

  • Estrogen → supports uterine growth

Exam pearl:
hCG = LH-like hormone that prevents corpus luteum degeneration in early pregnancy.

Physiology-02.question: ৪২) Which of the following hormones has the shortest plasma half-life?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is norepinephrine. Catecholamines have the shortest plasma half-life because they are rapidly metabolized by:

  • Monoamine oxidase (MAO)

  • Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)

The plasma half-life of norepinephrine is approximately 1–2 minutes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Corticosterone – A steroid hormone with a longer half-life (tens of minutes).

  • Renin – Plasma half-life is longer than catecholamines (about 10–20 minutes).

  • Aldosterone – Steroid hormone with a half-life of around 15–30 minutes.

High-yield points:

Approximate plasma half-life:

  • Norepinephrine → ~1–2 min (shortest)

  • Renin → ~10–20 min

  • Aldosterone → ~15–30 min

  • Cortisol/corticosterone → longer

Exam pearl:
Catecholamines = very short half-life due to rapid COMT and MAO metabolism.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৩) Excess ADH secretion may result in
৪৪) Thyroid hormone excess results in
৪৫) Most prevalent forms of calcium
৪৬) Blood levels of which of the following substances is decreased in Graves’ disease?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is TSH. In Graves’ disease, autoantibodies (TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies/TSI) stimulate the thyroid gland, causing:

  • ↑ T3

  • ↑ T4

  • ↓ TSH (due to negative feedback on the pituitary)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Triiodothyronine (T3) – Increased in Graves’ disease.

  • Thyroxine (T4) – Increased in Graves’ disease.

  • Iodide (I⁻) – Not the typical decreased parameter in Graves’ disease.

High-yield points:

Graves’ disease:

  • ↑ T3, ↑ T4

  • ↓ TSH

  • Positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb/TSI)

Exam pearl:
Primary hyperthyroidism = high thyroid hormones + suppressed TSH.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৭) Activator of pepsinogens
Physiology-02.exp:
.

The correct answer is H⁺ (hydrogen ion). Pepsinogen, secreted by chief cells of the stomach, is converted into active pepsin by exposure to the acidic gastric environment.

Mechanism:

  • Gastric parietal cells secrete HCl

  • HCl provides H⁺ ions

  • H⁺ converts pepsinogen → pepsin

  • Pepsin further activates more pepsinogen (autocatalytic activation)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • K⁺ – Present in gastric juice but does not activate pepsinogen.

  • HCl – Provides the acidic environment, but the active factor in conversion is H⁺.

  • Na⁺ – Does not activate pepsinogen.

High-yield points:

Pepsinogen activation:

  • Source → Chief cells

  • Activator → H⁺

  • Active enzyme → Pepsin

  • Function → Protein digestion

Exam pearl:
H⁺ activates pepsinogen into pepsin.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৮) Stimuli that inhibit gastrin secretion
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is somatostatin. Somatostatin, secreted by D cells of the stomach and pancreas, inhibits gastrin secretion from gastric G cells.

The other options are incorrect because they stimulate gastrin secretion:

  • Distention – Gastric stretching stimulates gastrin release via local reflexes.

  • Increased vagal discharge – Vagus nerve stimulates gastrin secretion through GRP (gastrin-releasing peptide).

  • Calcium – Stimulates gastrin secretion.

High-yield points:

Stimulators of gastrin:

  • Gastric distension

  • Vagal stimulation (GRP)

  • Peptides and amino acids

  • Calcium

Inhibitor of gastrin:

  • Somatostatin

  • Low gastric pH (acid feedback)

Exam pearl:
D-cell somatostatin inhibits G-cell gastrin secretion.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৯) Sucrase enzyme is derived from
৫০) Source of Pepsinogen
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is chief cell. Chief cells (zymogenic cells) of the gastric glands secrete:

  • Pepsinogen (inactive precursor of pepsin)

  • Gastric lipase

Pepsinogen is activated by H⁺ from gastric acid to form pepsin, which digests proteins.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Parietal cell – Secretes HCl and intrinsic factor.

  • G cell – Secretes gastrin.

  • EC cell (enterochromaffin cell) – Secretes serotonin and helps regulate GI motility.

High-yield points:

Gastric cell Secretion
Chief cell Pepsinogen
Parietal (oxyntic) cell HCl + intrinsic factor
G cell Gastrin
ECL cell Histamine

Exam pearl:
Chief cells produce pepsinogen; parietal cells produce HCl.
